full_judgment:
41. In Sadek Hossain Khan vs Hashim Ali Khan, AIR 1916 PC 27=43 1A the legitimacy of one Sultan Mirza came up for consideration. He claimed to be a son of Zohora Kainam, whom, he claimed, the Nowab had married in Mota form, Zohora Kainam was an Abyssinian slave girl and was brought home by the Nawab's father from Mecca. But the sons of the Nowab through his admitted wives averred that Zohora Kainam was not legally married to their father, and, as such, Sultan Mirza was not a legitimate son as claimed. It was found from evidence that the Nawab, during his lifetime, treated Sultan Mirza as his son in the marmer, which suggested his acknowledgement of Sultan Mirza as a legitimate son. But it was found that there was no lawful marriage between the Nawab and Zohora Kainam but that she was a mere mistress of the Nawab, and, as such, Sultan Mirza was not his legitimate son. In these circumstances it was observed by their Lordship of the Privy Council: 

 42. In Habibur Rahman Chowdhury vs Altaf Ali Chowdhury, AIR 1922 PC 159, their Lordships considered a similar question as to legitimacy viz-a-viz legitimation under the Muhammadan Law and observed that "legitimacy" is a status which results from certain facts, whereas "legitimation" is a procedure which creates a status which did not exist before and that under Muhammadan Law there is no legitimation because. Under Muhammadan Law, "a person to be legitimate son of another person must be the offspring of a marriage between his mother and his alleged father and that any other offspring is the off-spring of zina, that is, illicit connection and cannot be legitimate." In that case the appellant claimed to be a legitimate son of Abdus Sobhan, Nawab of Bogra, stating that he was born of Mozelle Cohen, a Jewish lady, who he claimed was a legally married wife of the Nawab. Nawab's grandson through the daughter of his first wife and others disputed the claim contending that Mozelle Cohen was never married to the Nawab. It was found from evidence that the Nawab lived and cohabited with her for a long time but she was never married to him, and that she was Nawab's concubine only. It was held that though the Nawab had acknowledged the appellant as his son during his lifetime no marriage between those parents having been provided, the appellant was not a legitimate son of the Nawab.
